title: The Text-Processing Toolkit
sub: grep, sort, sed, awk, jq and friends: reshape any text into the answer you need
goals: Select lines with grep and write regular expressions in BRE, ERE and Python-style flavours
Count, rank and de-duplicate data with sort, uniq and wc
Cut, join, compare and reformat text with cut, tr, paste, join, comm, diff and column
Edit streams with sed substitutions, addresses and capture groups
Write awk programs with fields, patterns, arrays and printf to sum, group and report
Turn messy logs, CSV and JSON into answers using multi-stage pipelines

blocks.text: Almost everything a computer tells you arrives as text: logs, command output, configuration files, CSV exports, API responses. The tools in this chapter treat that text as data. You will select the lines you care about, cut out the fields that matter, count and rank them, and print the result in the shape the next command expects. By the end you will be able to answer questions like "which client hammered the server, how many bytes did it pull, and in which minute?" with one line of shell, and you will know which tool to reach for first.

Open Terminal in `~/lab` (see [Setting up your lab](#setup) if the folder does not exist yet) and keep it open. This chapter uses `access.log`, `users.csv`, `ips.txt`, `ping.log`, `notes.txt`, `scan.txt` and `hosts.txt`. The practice terminal at the bottom of the page has the same files, so you can experiment there without touching anything on your Mac.
Text as records and fields

Every tool in this chapter shares one mental model. Input is a sequence of **records**, normally one per line, ended by a newline. Each record is a sequence of **fields** separated by a delimiter: whitespace in a log, a comma in a CSV, a colon in `/etc/passwd`, a `=` in a `key=value` pair. Tools differ in how they select records and how they cut fields, but the shape is always the same.
Because tools exchange plain lines, you choose a tool by asking what operation you need on the stream:

macOS ships the BSD versions of these programs. Most flags in this chapter work on Linux too, but a few differ: `sed -i` needs an empty suffix argument (`sed -i '' ...`), `grep -P` does not exist, `cut` cannot split on a multi-character delimiter, and `awk` is the minimalist "one true awk", which lacks GNU extras such as `gensub`, `asort` and `strftime`. Everything below is written for the macOS versions. If you install GNU tools with Homebrew they appear with a `g` prefix (`gsed`, `gawk`, `ggrep`) so that they never shadow the system ones.
Locale and sorting

`sort`, `grep -i` and character ranges all consult the locale. In a UTF-8 locale `sort` compares according to language rules (case is mostly ignored at first, punctuation may be skipped). In the **C locale** it compares raw byte values, which is faster and predictable. Prefix a command with `LC_ALL=C` to switch for that one command: `LC_ALL=C sort file`. Use it when the order must be identical across machines or when a script behaves differently in Terminal and in `cron`.
Finding lines: grep

`grep` reads lines, keeps those that match a pattern and writes them out. The name comes from the old `ed` command `g/re/p`: *globally search for a regular expression and print*. It is the first stage of most pipelines.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ grep ERROR notes.txt
ERROR: backup job failed on nas.lan (disk full)
ERROR: DNS lookup for update.example.com timed out
$ grep -i -n 'todo' notes.txt
3:TODO: replace the old router password
7:todo: label the ethernet cables
$ grep -c ' 404 ' access.log
11
$ grep -v -E '^(=|$)' notes.txt | head -4
Lab notebook
TODO: replace the old router password
Reminder: the Pi runs the DNS sinkhole
ERROR: backup job failed on nas.lan (disk full)

blocks.text: `grep` has three pattern dialects, chosen by flag, and mixing them up is the number one cause of "my regex does nothing":

head: Flag
Dialect
Metacharacters
rows: `. * [ ] ^ $` are special; `\( \) \{ \} \|` need backslashes (and `\|` and `\+` are extensions)
nothing is special; fastest, safest for literal text such as `1.2.3.4` or `a+b`

blocks.text: Use `-E` by default. It reads the way regexes are written in documentation and in Python, and it keeps your backslashes to a minimum.

blocks.name: grep
blocks.sum: Print the lines of its input that match a pattern, or the matching text itself with -o.
blocks.syntax: grep [-E|-F] [-i] [-v] [-n] [-c] [-o] [-w] [-l] [-r] [-h] [-A n] [-B n] [-C n] [-e pat] [-f patfile] [--include glob] pattern [file ...]

how.text: `grep` reads each line, tests it against the pattern and prints the lines that match. Its exit status is a three-way signal: 0 if any line matched, 1 if none did, 2 on an error such as an unreadable file. That makes it a condition as well as a filter: `if grep -q ERROR notes.txt; then ...` works with no output at all.

With no file arguments `grep` reads stdin, which is how it joins a pipeline. With several files it prefixes each line with the file name; `-h` suppresses the prefix and `-l` lists only the names of files that matched. `-r` walks a directory tree.
`-o` changes what is printed from "the whole line" to "only the part that matched, one match per line". Combined with a good regex it extracts data (IPs, URLs, numbers) from messy text.

flags.d: Extended regular expressions: `+ ? | ( ) { }` work without backslashes.
Treat the pattern as a fixed string, not a regex. With `-f file` it matches every line of the file as a literal.
Ignore case.
Invert: print the lines that do not match.
Prefix each output line with its line number.
Print only the count of matching lines (per file).
Print only the matched part of each line, one per line.
Match whole words only: the match must be bounded by non-word characters.
Print only the names of files that contain a match.
Recurse into directories. Add `--include='*.log'` to limit the files searched.
Print n lines of trailing context after each match; `-B n` is leading context, `-C n` both.
Read patterns from a file, one per line; a line matches if any pattern matches.
Suppress file name prefixes when searching several files.

examples.out:
5:ERROR: backup job failed on nas.lan (disk full)

anat.exp: three groups of 1-3 digits and a dot, then a final 1-3 digit group

gotchas: `grep -c` counts matching **lines**, not matches. A line with three hits counts once. Use `grep -o ... | wc -l` to count matches.
Without `-E`, `grep 'a|b'` searches for the literal text `a|b`. Some implementations accept `\|` in a basic regex, but portable scripts write `-E 'a|b'`.
The pattern can start with `-`. Protect it with `--`: `grep -- '-v' file`.
notes: macOS `grep` also understands `--color=auto`; `export GREP_COLORS` or `alias grep='grep --color=auto'` is a common `.zshrc` line.

blocks.text: Regular expressions

A **regular expression** (regex) is a small language for describing sets of strings. `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `less`, your editor and Python's `re` module all use it, with minor dialect differences. Learn it once and it pays off for the rest of your career.
The pieces

head: Piece
Meaning
Example
Matches
rows: start and end of the line
one character not in the set
POSIX class: also `alpha alnum upper lower space punct`
zero or more of the previous item
group, and remember the match for `\1`
a backslash makes a metacharacter literal
word boundary, word char, digit: **Python and PCRE only**
digits in Python, not in BRE/ERE

blocks.text: Precedence works the way arithmetic does: repetition binds tightest, then concatenation, then alternation. `ab|cd` means `(ab)|(cd)`, and `ab*` means `a(b*)`. Use parentheses to group.

blocks.title: Reading a regex from left to right

tokens.exp: group: one to three digits followed by a literal dot, repeated exactly three times
a fourth run of one to three digits with no dot

blocks.text: Greedy and lazy

Quantifiers are **greedy**: they take as much as they can and give back only if the rest of the pattern fails. On the line `"GET /a HTTP/1.1" 200 "-"`, the pattern `".*"` matches from the first quote to the **last** one, not to the next one. Fixes that work everywhere: exclude the delimiter with a negated class, `"[^"]*"`. In Python and PCRE you can also use the lazy form `".*?"`. BRE and ERE have no lazy quantifier, which is one more reason to prefer negated classes.
The three flavours you will meet

head: Feature
BRE (`grep`, `sed`)
ERE (`grep -E`, `sed -E`, `awk`)
Python `re` / PCRE
rows: undefined in POSIX, many tools allow it

blocks.text: Linux tutorials use `grep -P '\d+'` for Perl-compatible patterns. BSD grep on macOS rejects `-P`. Use `grep -E '[0-9]+'`, or reach for Python (`python3 -c`, [Python and files](#py-files) covers `re` in depth) or `rg` (ripgrep, below) when you need lookahead or lazy matching.

blocks.title: Test patterns before you trust them

blocks.text: Paste a line from `access.log` into the tester above and try `^[0-9.]+`, then `"[^"]*"`, then `" ([0-9]{3}) "`. Then run the same `grep -Eo` on the real file. A regex you have seen match and fail on sample data is a regex you can debug.
Ordering and counting: sort, uniq, wc

Counting things is the most common reason to reach for these tools. The core trio is `sort`, `uniq -c` and `wc -l`, and `uniq` needs sorted input because it only merges adjacent duplicates (see the gotcha in [Streams, Redirection & Pipes](#pipes)).

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ sort ips.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -4
   4 10.0.0.5
   3 192.168.1.50
   3 10.0.0.12
   2 192.168.1.1
$ sort ips.txt | uniq -d
1.1.1.1
10.0.0.12
10.0.0.5
172.16.0.9
192.168.1.1
192.168.1.50
$ cut -d, -f4 users.csv | tail -n +2 | sort -n | tail -3
5432
8000
8080
$ wc -l access.log ips.txt hosts.txt
     120 access.log
      23 ips.txt
      10 hosts.txt
     153 total

blocks.name: sort
blocks.sum: Sort lines of text, by whole line or by a chosen field, as text or as numbers.

how.text: `sort` reads all of its input, orders the lines and writes them out. Because it must see every line before it can print the first, it is the one stage in a pipeline that cannot stream. Large inputs spill to temporary files automatically.

The default comparison is text, in the current locale. Numbers need `-n`, otherwise `10` sorts before `9`. `-k` picks the sort key: `-k2,2` means "from field 2 to the end of field 2", and the `,2` matters, because `-k2` alone means "from field 2 to the end of the line". Give each key its own options when mixing types: `-k1,1 -k2,2nr`.

With `-t` you name the field separator; without it, fields are separated by runs of blanks. `-u` drops duplicates according to the key, keeping the first of each group. `-s` makes the sort **stable**, so lines with equal keys keep their input order.

flags.d: Compare numerically (leading blanks and a sign are understood).
Compare human-readable sizes such as `2K 1M 3G`.
Reverse the order.
Output only the first of each run of equal keys.
Sort by the key from field a to field b; append `n`, `r` or `f` to a key for per-key options.
Use the character c as the field separator.
Fold lower case to upper case when comparing (case-insensitive).
Stable sort: keep the original order of equal lines.
Write to a file. Safe even if the file is also the input.

examples.desc: Rank users by port, highest first
Sort IP addresses correctly, octet by octet

Sort by one field, then count it
examples.code: tail -n +2 users.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

gotchas: `sort -n` on `10.0.0.5` reads only the leading `10`. Sorting addresses needs the four-key form above.
`sort file > file` empties the file first. Use `sort -o file file`.

blocks.name: uniq
blocks.sum: Collapse runs of identical adjacent lines, optionally counting them.

how.text: `uniq` compares each line with the one before it. Equal neighbours collapse into one, so unsorted input keeps its duplicates. Put `sort` in front, or use `sort -u` when you do not need counts.

The counting form `uniq -c` prefixes each surviving line with the length of its run, right-aligned in a fixed-width column. `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` is the standard way to build a frequency table. `-d` prints one copy of each line that was repeated, `-u` prints only lines that were never repeated.

flags.d: Prefix each line with the number of times it occurred.
Print only lines that occur more than once (one copy each).
Print only lines that occur exactly once.
Compare ignoring case.
Skip the first n whitespace-separated fields when comparing.
Skip the first n characters when comparing.

Frequency table of IPs
Count lines per status code while ignoring the IP in field 1

gotchas: The count column is padded with spaces. Strip it with `awk '{print $1}'` or `sed 's/^ *//'` before using it in a comparison.

blocks.name: wc
blocks.sum: Count lines, words, characters and bytes.

how.text: `wc` makes one pass over its input and reports counts. With no flags it prints lines, words and bytes. `-l` counts newline characters, so a final line with no trailing newline is not counted. `-c` counts bytes and `-m` counts characters; they differ for UTF-8 text such as `é`, which is two bytes but one character.

flags.d: Number of lines.
Number of words (runs of non-blank characters).
Number of bytes.
Number of characters in the current locale.

examples.desc: How many lines in each file?
Count distinct clients
Print just the number, with no padding for use in a comparison

gotchas: `wc -l file` prints the name, `wc -l < file` does not. macOS pads the number with spaces either way.

blocks.text: Shaping lines: cut, tr, paste, join, comm, diff

These tools each do one small job. They matter because they are fast, predictable and available on every Unix machine you will ever log into, including the ones that have no `awk` scripts or Python installed.

blocks.name: cut
blocks.sum: Keep selected fields or character positions from every line.

how.text: `cut` is a column selector. With `-f` it splits each line at a **single-character** delimiter (`-d`, default tab) and prints the chosen fields; with `-c` it prints chosen character positions. Lists are comma separated and may contain ranges: `-f1,3`, `-f2-`, `-c1-8`.

`cut` never collapses repeated delimiters. In text aligned with several spaces, each space is a delimiter and you get empty fields. Use `awk` for that kind of data. Lines without the delimiter are printed whole unless you add `-s`.

flags.d: Field delimiter, one character. Default is tab.
Fields to keep, such as `1,3` or `2-`.
Character positions to keep.
With `-f`, skip lines that contain no delimiter.

examples.desc: Names and ports from the CSV
Only the date part of each log timestamp
List the distinct roles
Pull usernames out of /etc/passwd

gotchas: `cut -d' ' -f2` on `a   b` (three spaces) returns an empty string. `awk '{print $2}'` returns `b`.

blocks.name: tr
blocks.sum: Translate, squeeze or delete individual characters read from stdin.

how.text: `tr` works on characters, not lines or patterns, and **only reads stdin**, so you always write `tr ... < file` or `cmd | tr ...`. With two sets it replaces each character of `set1` by the character in the same position of `set2`. With `-d` it deletes characters in `set1`. With `-s` it squeezes runs of a repeated character from `set1` into one.
Sets accept ranges (`a-z`), classes (`[:upper:]`, `[:space:]`, `[:digit:]`) and escapes such as `\n`, `\t` and `\r`.

flags.d: Delete characters in set1.
Squeeze repeated characters in set1 into a single one.
Use the complement of set1 (everything except those characters).

examples.desc: Upper-case a file
Remove Windows carriage returns
Turn a comma-separated list into one item per line
Collapse runs of spaces so that cut works on aligned text

gotchas: `tr abc xyz` maps characters, it never replaces the word `abc`. For words use `sed`.

blocks.name: paste
blocks.sum: Merge lines of files side by side, or join all lines of one file into one row.

how.text: `paste` glues corresponding lines of its inputs together with a tab (or `-d`). With `-s` it works down one file instead, turning its lines into a single row. The name `-` stands for stdin and may be repeated: `paste - - -` groups every three input lines into one row.

flags.d: Use these delimiter characters instead of tab, cycling through them.
Serial mode: paste the lines of each file into one row.

blocks.name: join
blocks.sum: Combine two sorted files by matching a key field, like a database join.
blocks.syntax: join [-t sep] [-1 field] [-2 field] [-a 1|2] [-v 1|2] [-o list] file1 file2

how.text: `join` reads two files that are **both sorted on the join field** and prints one output line for each pair of lines with equal keys: the key first, then the remaining fields of file1, then of file2. If either file is not sorted on that field with the same collating rules, `join` silently drops matches, so sort first (and use `LC_ALL=C` on both sorts if in doubt).
`-a 1` also prints unmatched lines of file1 (a left join), and `-v 1` prints only the unmatched ones, which finds records with no partner.

flags.d: Field separator for input and output (default is blanks).
Join on field n of file 1.
Join on field n of file 2.
Also print unpairable lines from file n.
Print only unpairable lines from file n.
Choose output fields, such as `1.1,1.2,2.2`.

blocks.name: comm
blocks.sum: Compare two sorted files and show lines unique to each and lines common to both.

how.text: `comm` prints three columns: lines only in file1, lines only in file2, and lines in both. Each flag **suppresses** a column, so `comm -12` shows only the common lines (set intersection), `comm -23` only those unique to file1 (set difference), and `comm -3` everything that differs. Both inputs must be sorted.

Suppress column 2 (lines only in file2).
Suppress column 3 (lines in both).

blocks.name: diff
blocks.sum: Show the line-by-line differences between two files or directories.

how.text: `diff` finds a shortest set of line insertions and deletions that turns `old` into `new`. The default output uses `3c3` style hunks; `-u` produces the **unified** format you see in `git diff`, with three lines of context, `-` for removed lines and `+` for added lines. The exit status is 0 when the files are identical, 1 when they differ, 2 on trouble, so `diff -q a b > /dev/null` works as a test.

flags.d: Unified format with context.
Recurse into directories.
Only report whether files differ.
Side-by-side output.
Ignore case differences.
Ignore all white space.

Compare the sorted contents of two commands without temp files

blocks.name: column
blocks.sum: Align text into neat columns.

how.text: With `-t`, `column` measures each field and pads the rows into an aligned table. The input separator is whitespace unless you set `-s`. It is a display tool: use it as the last stage of a pipeline to make results readable, not to produce data for another program.

blocks.name: rev
blocks.sum: Reverse the characters of each line.

how.text: `rev` writes every line backwards. Its main use in pipelines is to get "the last field" when fields have a variable count: reverse, cut the first field, reverse again.

blocks.sum: Number the lines of a file.

how.text: `nl` prefixes each line with a line number. By default it numbers only non-empty lines (`-b t`); `-b a` numbers all lines. It is handy for referring to a line when you discuss output with someone, or for feeding numbers to `sed -n 'Np'`.

blocks.name: fold
blocks.sum: Wrap long lines at a fixed width.

how.text: `fold` breaks lines that exceed the width (default 80 columns), even in the middle of a word. With `-s` it breaks at the last space instead. It works on lines one by one and never joins anything.

blocks.name: fmt
blocks.sum: Reflow paragraphs to a target width.

how.text: Unlike `fold`, `fmt` treats a block of text as a paragraph: it joins lines and then breaks them again so that every line is close to the goal width. Blank lines separate paragraphs. Use it for text, never for code or tables.

blocks.text: Editing streams: sed

`sed` (stream editor) reads one line at a time into a buffer called the **pattern space**, applies a list of commands, prints the result and moves on. It never loads the whole file, which is why it works on gigabytes. Its everyday job is **substitution**.

tokens.exp: script: s, then pattern, replacement and flags separated by /
pattern with two capture groups around a literal dot
replacement: second group, a dot, then the first group
flag: replace every match on the line, not only the first

blocks.text: The part before the command is an **address**: which lines the command applies to. With no address a command applies to every line.

head: Address
Selects
Example
rows: from a match of a through the next match of b

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ sed 's/\.org/.example/' hosts.txt | head -3
example.com
python.example
github.com
$ sed -n '3,5p' notes.txt
TODO: replace the old router password
Reminder: the Pi runs the DNS sinkhole
ERROR: backup job failed on nas.lan (disk full)
$ sed -E 's/^([A-Za-z]+):.*/\1/' notes.txt | head -4
Lab notebook
============
TODO
Reminder
$ sed '/^$/d;/^=/d' notes.txt | head -3
Lab notebook
TODO: replace the old router password
Reminder: the Pi runs the DNS sinkhole

blocks.name: sed
blocks.sum: Apply editing commands such as substitute, delete and print to every selected line of a stream.

how.text: For each input line `sed` copies the line to the pattern space, runs every command whose address matches, and (unless `-n` is given) prints the pattern space. The commands you will use: `s/re/new/flags` substitute, `d` delete the line, `p` print it, `q` quit. Flags for `s`: `g` all matches, a number such as `2` the second match, `p` print if substituted.

In the replacement, `&` is the whole match and `\1` to `\9` are capture groups from the pattern. Any character can replace `/` as delimiter, which saves escaping when the pattern holds slashes: `s|/usr/local|/opt/homebrew|`.
Several commands combine with `;` or with multiple `-e`. `-n` suppresses automatic printing, so `sed -n '/x/p'` behaves like `grep x`.

flags.d: Do not print the pattern space automatically; only `p` prints.
Extended regex syntax: `( ) + ? |` without backslashes.
Add a script; may be repeated.
Read the script from a file.
Edit the file in place on macOS. The empty string is the backup suffix; `-i .bak` keeps a backup copy.

Print lines 3 to 5

examples.code: sed -E 's/.*"[A-Z]+ ([^ ]+) HTTP.*/\1/' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

anat.exp: greedy prefix, capture the path after the method, discard the rest, print the capture

gotchas: BSD `sed -i` requires an argument after it. `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` fails on macOS with "invalid command code"; write `sed -i '' ...` (no backup) or `sed -i '.bak' ...`. This differs from GNU sed, so scripts shared with Linux users need care.
BSD `sed` does not understand `\n` or `\t` in the replacement. To insert a tab, use zsh's `$'\t'` quoting: `sed $'s/,/\t/g' file`.
`sed 's/a/b/'` replaces only the first match per line. Add `g` for all.
Without `-E`, `+`, `?`, `|` and `( )` are literal characters in the pattern. Forgetting `-E` is the common reason a substitution does nothing.

blocks.text: awk: a language for fields

`awk` is a small programming language built for line-oriented data. A program is a list of **pattern { action }** pairs. For every input line `awk` splits the record into fields, then runs the action of each pair whose pattern matches. If you leave out the pattern the action runs for every line; if you leave out the action the default is `{ print }`.

blocks.code:
awk 'BEGIN { ... }      pattern { action }      pattern { action }      END { ... }'  file

   │                      │                                              │
   runs once, before      runs for every input line, in order            runs once, after the last line
   any input is read      fields $1 $2 ... $NF are already split         (totals and reports go here)

blocks.text: Fields and built-in variables

head: Variable
Holds
Example
rows: the fields of the current line
number of fields on this line
`$NF` is the last field, `$(NF-1)` the one before it
number of the current record, counting across all files
record number within the current file
input field separator (default: runs of blanks)
output field separator used by `print a, b` (default a space)
record separators for input and output (default newline)

blocks.text: Fields can be assigned to. When you modify any field, `awk` rebuilds `$0` with `OFS` between fields: `awk 'BEGIN{OFS=","} {$1=$1} 1'` converts whitespace-separated data into CSV in one line. The trailing `1` is a pattern that is always true, so the default action `print` runs.
Patterns
A pattern decides whether the action runs. The common forms:

items.text: **Regex**: `/ERROR/` matches lines containing ERROR. `$9 ~ /^4/` tests one field; `$9 !~ /^2/` is the negation.
**Comparison**: `$9 >= 400`, `$10 > 50000`, `$1 == "10.0.0.5"`. Fields that look numeric compare as numbers, otherwise as strings.
**Range**: `/START/,/END/` runs for every line from one match through the next.

blocks.text: Variables, arithmetic and associative arrays

Variables need no declaration. They start as `0` (and as `""`), so `sum += $10` works from the first line. Arithmetic uses `+ - * / % ^`; all numbers are floating point. **Associative arrays** are maps from any string to a value, created on first use, and they are what turns `awk` from a field printer into a grouping engine.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk '{s += $10} END {print s, s/NR}' access.log
1700295 14169.1
$ awk '{c[$9]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort
200 57
301 14
302 6
304 10
401 12
403 8
404 11
500 2
$ awk -F, 'NR > 1 {n[$2]++; p[$2] = p[$2] " " $4} END {for (r in n) print r, n[r], p[r]}' users.csv | sort
admin 2  22 443
dev 4  8080 22 443 8000
guest 2  80 80
ops 2  445 5432
$ awk '$9 == 404 && $7 ~ /admin|wp-/ {print $1, $7}' access.log | head -3
203.0.113.7 /wp-login.php
185.220.101.4 /admin
198.51.100.23 /admin

blocks.text: `for (k in arr)` visits keys in an order the implementation chooses. It can differ between the on-page terminal, macOS `awk` and `gawk`. Pipe the output through `sort` whenever order matters, as above. The loop variable holds the **key**; the value is `arr[k]`.
printf and the built-in functions

`print a, b` joins with `OFS` and ends with a newline. `printf "format", args...` gives full control and prints no newline unless you add `\n`, like the `printf` of [zsh basics](#zsh-basics): `%s` string, `%d` integer, `%.2f` two decimals, `%-15s` left-aligned in 15 columns, `%5d` right-aligned in 5.

blocks.name: awk
blocks.sum: Run a small program over each line of text, with automatic field splitting, patterns, arrays and printf.

how.text: `awk` reads input one record at a time, splits it into fields on `FS`, and for every `pattern { action }` pair in the program whose pattern is true runs the action. `BEGIN` blocks run before input, `END` blocks after. Variables are created on first use, strings and numbers convert automatically, and associative arrays hold any key-to-value mapping, so grouping, counting and summing are a few characters each.

The macOS `awk` is the minimal "one true awk" (a 2020 build on recent releases; `awk --version` shows it). It supports everything in this chapter. It lacks GNU additions such as `gensub`, `asort`, `asorti`, `strftime`, `systime` and `PROCINFO`. If you need those, `brew install gawk` and call `gawk`.
Quote the program with single quotes so the shell does not touch the `$1` and braces. To pass a shell variable in, use `-v name="$value"` rather than splicing it into the program text.

flags.d: Set the input field separator. A single character, a string, or a regex such as `-F'[,;]'`.
Set an awk variable before the program starts (available in `BEGIN`).
Read the program from a file.

examples.code: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) if (c[ip] > 10) print ip, c[ip]}' access.log | sort -k2 -rn

gotchas: Assigning `$3 = "x"` rebuilds the line with `OFS`, which collapses runs of spaces. Print `$0` before modifying fields if you need the original text.
Unquoted regexes inside single quotes still need backslashes for dots: `$1 ~ /^10\.0\./`.
`awk '$9 == 404'` compares as numbers when both sides look numeric. `$1 == 10` against the string `10.0.0.5` compares as text and is false.

blocks.name: awk functions
blocks.sum: The built-in functions of awk: string, regex, numeric and array helpers.
blocks.syntax: length(s)  substr(s,i,n)  index(s,t)  split(s,a,sep)  sub(re,r,t)  gsub(re,r,t)  match(s,re)  tolower(s)  toupper(s)  sprintf(fmt,...)  int(x)  sqrt(x)

how.text: String positions count from 1, not 0. `substr(s, i, n)` returns n characters starting at i. `split(s, arr, sep)` fills `arr[1]..arr[n]` and returns n; the separator can be a regex. `sub` and `gsub` substitute in place in the target (default `$0`) and return the number of replacements; `&` in the replacement means the matched text. `match(s, re)` returns the start position, or 0, and sets `RSTART` and `RLENGTH`, which lets you cut the matched piece out with `substr`. `length(arr)` returns the number of elements of an array.

examples.desc: Lower-case the first field and show its length
Strip the time= prefix from ping lines
Pull the hour out of the log timestamp with match and substr
examples.code: awk '{ if (match($4, /:[0-9][0-9]:/)) print substr($4, RSTART + 1, 2) }' access.log | head -2

examples.desc: Percentage of requests that were client errors
Domain names and their top-level domain
examples.code: awk '{n = split($1, p, "."); print $1, p[n]}' hosts.txt | head -3

blocks.text: JSON, bytes and fast search: jq, xxd, base64, rg, fzf
Line tools break down on nested or binary data. The tools below fill those gaps and slot into the same pipelines.

blocks.name: jq
blocks.sum: Read JSON and select, filter and reshape it with a small expression language.

how.text: `jq` parses JSON on stdin and applies a **filter**. The filter `.` is the whole document, `.name` selects a key, `.a.b` goes deeper, `.[0]` takes an array element and `.[]` unpacks every element into a stream of outputs. Filters combine with `|` inside the quotes, just like the shell pipe: `.[] | select(.p == 22) | .n`. `select(cond)` keeps values for which the condition is true, `map(f)` applies f to each array element, and `[ ... ]` collects outputs back into an array.

By default strings print with their JSON quotes. `-r` (raw) removes them, which you need whenever the result feeds another command. `-c` prints each result on one line, so line-oriented tools can process it.

flags.d: Raw output: print strings without quotes.
Compact output: one result per line.
Exit with status 1 if the last output is `false` or `null` (for use in `if`).
Slurp: read all inputs into one array.

examples.desc: Read a nested value
Keep only the entries whose port is 22
JSON array to tab-separated rows for awk or column
List repository names from the GitHub API

gotchas: Without `-r`, `jq '.name'` prints `"pi.lan"` with quotes, which is wrong as an argument to another command.
notes: Recent macOS releases may ship a `jq` in `/usr/bin`; run `which jq` to see what you have. Install the current one with `brew install jq`.

blocks.name: xxd
blocks.sum: Show data as a hex dump, or turn hex back into bytes.

how.text: `xxd` prints offsets, hexadecimal bytes and the printable characters beside them. With `-p` it prints plain continuous hex, and `-r` reverses the operation. It is the quickest way to answer "what bytes are really in this file?", for example when invisible characters such as carriage returns or a byte-order mark break a script.

flags.d: Plain hex stream without offsets or text.
Reverse: convert hex back into binary.
Stop after n bytes.
Bytes per row (default 16).

examples.desc: Look at the first bytes of a file
Does this file have Windows line endings?

blocks.name: base64
blocks.sum: Encode bytes as printable text, or decode them.

how.text: Base64 represents arbitrary bytes with 64 printable characters so they survive text channels such as HTTP headers and JSON. It is an encoding, not encryption: anyone can reverse it. Basic auth in HTTP is the username and password joined by a colon, then base64 encoded.

flags.d: Decode. Older macOS releases spelled this `-D`; recent ones accept both.
Read from a file instead of stdin.

examples.desc: Encode a string without a trailing newline
Decode and read it

gotchas: `echo 'text' | base64` encodes the newline `echo` adds. Use `printf` or `echo -n` for exact input.

blocks.name: rg
blocks.sum: ripgrep: a fast recursive search that respects .gitignore and prints readable results.

how.text: `rg` searches a directory tree recursively by default, skips hidden files and anything your `.gitignore` excludes, and uses Rust regex syntax, which includes `\d`, lazy quantifiers and Unicode classes but no lookaround (the `-P` flag enables PCRE2 lookaround when your build includes it). It is the practical answer to "find this string somewhere in my project".

flags.d: Ignore case.
List only the files that match.
Include or exclude paths by glob, such as `-g '*.py'`.
Limit to a file type, such as `-t py`.

Files mentioning a host, counted

blocks.name: fzf
blocks.sum: An interactive fuzzy filter: pipe any list in, type to narrow it, press Enter to emit the choice.

how.text: `fzf` reads lines from stdin, shows them in a searchable list, and writes the selected line to stdout when you press Enter. That makes it a human-in-the-loop stage for a pipeline. After `brew install fzf`, run `$(brew --prefix)/opt/fzf/install` to enable the `⌃R` history search and `⌃T` file picker in zsh.

Show command output for the highlighted line; `{}` stands for it.

blocks.text: Recipes: answering real questions
Each recipe below is a pipeline you can build one stage at a time. Run them after every `|` until they look right.
Top talkers and a status histogram
Bytes per client and requests per minute
Counting lines is `uniq -c`. Adding a column per key needs an array:
The second command splits the timestamp field `[07/Oct/2026:09:14:08` on colons, so `t[2]` is the hour and `t[3]` the minute. The key `09:14` collects every request in that minute.
Parsing ping output
`ping.log` holds ten probes, one lost. The summary line carries what you need, and the per-probe lines let you compute your own numbers:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ grep -c 'time=' ping.log
9
$ grep 'time=' ping.log | sed -E 's/.*time=([0-9.]+) ms/\1/' | sort -n | sed -n '1p;$p'
11.205
16.102
$ awk '/time=/ {split($7,a,"="); s+=a[2]; n++} END {printf "avg %.2f ms over %d replies\n", s/n, n}' ping.log
avg 12.94 ms over 9 replies
$ awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}' ping.log
10.0%

blocks.text: The `sed -n '1p;$p'` stage prints the first and last line of the sorted values, which is the minimum and maximum.
Extracting IPs from messy text

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ grep -Eoh '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' notes.txt scan.txt | sort -u
192.168.1.1
192.168.1.50
192.168.1.60
192.168.1.70
192.168.1.90
$ grep -Eoh '[a-z0-9.-]+\.lan' scan.txt notes.txt | sort | uniq -c
   1 homeassistant.lan
   2 nas.lan
   3 pi.lan
   2 printer.lan
   1 router.lan

blocks.text: Remember that this regex matches anything that looks like four numbers, including `999.999.999.999`. For strict validation use Python's `ipaddress` module ([Python files and pipelines](#py-files)).
CSV math

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk -F, 'NR > 1 {s[$2] += $4; n[$2]++} END {for (r in s) printf "%-6s %d users, port sum %d\n", r, n[r], s[r]}' users.csv | sort
admin  2 users, port sum 465
dev    4 users, port sum 16545
guest  2 users, port sum 160
ops    2 users, port sum 5877
$ awk -F, 'NR > 1 && $2 > 1250 {print $1, $2}' data/report-2026-09.csv
2 1315
4 1402
5 1290
$ awk -F, 'NR > 1 {e += $3; r += $2} END {printf "error rate %.2f%%\n", 100 * e / r}' data/report-2026-09.csv
error rate 1.16%

blocks.text: Plain `-F,` does not handle commas inside quoted CSV fields. For real-world CSV with quotes, use Python's `csv` module or a CSV-aware tool. The lab files have no quoted commas, so `-F,` is safe here.
Finding duplicates
`uniq -d` shows each repeated line once. `awk 'seen[$0]++'` prints each *extra* occurrence, because the post-increment returns the old count: 0 (false) the first time, positive afterwards.
Common mistakes

Cause
Fix

blocks.title: Test destructive sed on a copy

blocks.text: `sed -i` rewrites the file in place with no undo. Run the substitution without `-i` first and check the output, then repeat with `-i '.bak'` so that a backup exists. Never run `sed -i` against a file you cannot recreate.
Practice
Work in `~/lab`. Build each pipeline one stage at a time and look at the data after every `|`.

blocks.title: Distinct roles

task.text: Print each distinct `role` in `users.csv`, one per line, sorted. The header row must not appear.

hints: The role is field 2 and the delimiter is a comma.

why.text: `tail -n +2` removes the header, `cut` selects the column and `sort -u` sorts and de-duplicates in one stage.

blocks.verify: [[ $(tail -n +2 users.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ') == 4 ]] && echo OK

blocks.title: Status code histogram

task.text: Count the responses for each HTTP status code in `access.log`, most common first, as aligned columns.

hints: The status is field 9 of each line.
blocks.solution: awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | column -t

why.text: Extract, group, count, rank, format. This is the shape of most log questions: swap the extracted field to get paths, agents or methods.

blocks.title: The noisiest hour

task.text: Which minute of the day contains the most requests in `access.log`? Print the minute (`HH:MM`) and its count.

hints: Field 4 looks like `[07/Oct/2026:09:14:08`. Split it on `:`.
Use an array keyed by hour and minute, then rank with `sort -k2 -rn | head -1`.
blocks.solution: awk '{split($4, t, ":"); m[t[2] ":" t[3]]++} END {for (k in m) print k, m[k]}' access.log | sort -k2 -rn | head -1

why.text: `split` breaks the timestamp into parts, the array counts per key, and the final `sort` ranks the aggregate that `awk` produced.

blocks.title: Bytes by status class

task.text: Sum the bytes (field 10) of `access.log` separately for each first digit of the status code (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx) and print one line per class such as `2xx 1234567`.

hints: Build the key with `substr($9,1,1) "xx"` and add `$10` to that array element.
blocks.solution: awk '{k = substr($9, 1, 1) "xx"; b[k] += $10} END {for (k in b) print k, b[k]}' access.log | sort

why.text: Any expression can be an array key. Concatenating a literal turns a digit into a readable label.

task.text: Print `hosts.txt` with every `.org` replaced by `.example` and every `.com` replaced by `.test`, without changing the file.

why.text: `sed` applies each expression to every line in order. Escape the dot, otherwise it matches any character.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: the unsorted uniq

task.text: Run `uniq -c ips.txt` and note that many duplicate addresses still appear. Then fix the pipeline so each address appears once with its correct count, and explain why the first version was wrong.

hints: `uniq` only merges lines that are next to each other.
blocks.solution:
uniq -c ips.txt | head -5
sort ips.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

why.text: Without `sort`, equal addresses are scattered through the file and `uniq` sees each one as a new line. Sorting makes equal lines adjacent.

blocks.title: Find the quiet clients

task.text: List the client IPs in `access.log` that made fewer than five requests, with their counts, sorted by IP.

hints: Count first with an array, filter in the `END` loop.
blocks.solution: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) if (c[ip] < 5) print ip, c[ip]}' access.log | sort

why.text: Aggregating inside `awk` lets you filter on the count, which `uniq -c | grep` can only do with fragile pattern matching.

blocks.title: IPs in the log but not in the inventory

task.text: `ips.txt` is your inventory. Print the client addresses in `access.log` that are **not** listed in it, one per line.

hints: Both lists must be sorted and unique before `comm`.
Use process substitution so you need no temporary files. `comm -23` keeps lines only in the first input.

why.text: `comm` is a set operation. Column 1 holds lines unique to the first input; suppressing columns 2 and 3 leaves exactly the set difference.

blocks.title: Average and worst ping

task.text: From `ping.log`, print the average and the maximum round-trip time of the replies that arrived, in the form `avg=12.94 max=16.102`.

hints: The time is field 7 and looks like `time=11.842`.
`split($7, a, "=")` gives the number as `a[2]`. Track the largest in a variable.
blocks.solution: awk '/time=/ {split($7, a, "="); v = a[2] + 0; s += v; n++; if (v > m) m = v} END {printf "avg=%.2f max=%s\n", s / n, m}' ping.log

why.text: `+ 0` forces a numeric comparison. The `END` block turns accumulated totals into the report.

blocks.title: Strict IP extraction

task.text: From `notes.txt` and `scan.txt` together, print every distinct IPv4-looking token once, then count how many there are.

hints: `grep -Eo` with the dotted pattern prints one match per line.
blocks.solution:
grep -Eoh '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' notes.txt scan.txt | sort -u
grep -Eoh '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' notes.txt scan.txt | sort -u | wc -l

why.text: `-h` removes file-name prefixes that would otherwise break `sort -u`, and `-o` emits each match on its own line.

blocks.title: Convert a table to CSV

task.text: Turn the output of `awk '{print $1, $9, $10}' access.log | head -5` into comma-separated lines using one more pipeline stage of your choice.

hints: You can change the output separator, or translate spaces to commas.
blocks.solution:
awk 'BEGIN {OFS=","} {print $1, $9, $10}' access.log | head -5
awk '{print $1, $9, $10}' access.log | head -5 | tr ' ' ','

why.text: Setting `OFS` changes how `print a, b` joins its arguments. `tr` does the same change after the fact, but breaks if a field itself contains spaces.

questions.q: What does `awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$3} END {print s}' data.csv` print?

options.text: The third field of the last line
The sum of column 3, skipping the header
The sum of column 3 including the header

questions.why: `NR>1` skips line 1, the action accumulates field 3, and `END` prints the total once all input has been read.

questions.q: Which grep invocation extracts only the matched part of each line?
questions.why: `-o` prints only the matching text, one match per line. `-c` counts lines, `-v` inverts and `-l` lists file names.

questions.q: In `awk '{c[$9]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}'`, what does `k` hold inside the loop?

options.text: The key, here the status code

questions.why: In `for (k in arr)` the loop variable receives each key. The value is `arr[k]`.

questions.q: The pattern `".*"` is run on `"GET /a" 200 "-"`. How much does it match?

options.text: From the first quote to the last quote of the line

questions.why: `.*` is greedy and takes as much as it can while still letting the final `"` match. Use `"[^"]*"` to stop at the next quote.

questions.q: Which flag makes `sed` edit a file in place on macOS without keeping a backup?
questions.why: BSD `sed` requires an argument after `-i`. An empty string means no backup; `-i .bak` keeps one. GNU `sed -i` takes no argument, which is the difference that breaks Linux scripts on a Mac.

questions.q: Why does `grep 'a|b' file` find nothing on lines containing `a`?

options.text: Without `-E`, `|` is a literal character in a basic regex

questions.why: In BRE, `|` has no special meaning (some implementations use `\|`). `grep -E 'a|b'` enables alternation.

blocks.text: Try it in the practice terminal
The terminal runs the same text tools against the lab files. Missions check your output, so any correct pipeline passes. Try the awk idioms from the table above, then rebuild the recipes from memory.
**Next:** [Shell Scripting](#scripting) turns these pipelines into scripts with variables, tests, loops and functions, and builds `netcheck.zsh`, your first network tool.

terms.def: One unit of input, usually a line, that a tool processes as a whole
One piece of a record, separated from the others by a delimiter such as whitespace or a comma
Regular expression: a compact pattern language that describes sets of strings
Basic regular expression: the default dialect of grep and sed, where `\( \)` makes groups
Extended regular expression: `grep -E` and `sed -E` syntax with `+ ? | ( )` unescaped
A quantifier that matches as much text as possible before giving back
Part of a pattern in parentheses whose matched text can be reused as `\1` or `\2`
The buffer in which sed holds the current line while commands run
A map from string keys to values, created on first use in awk
A regex element such as `^` or `$` that matches a position, not a character
awk's output field separator, the string `print a, b` puts between its arguments
A sort that keeps lines with equal keys in their original order
